0. Input

Program:

int[] a = {5, 10, 15};
for (int i = 0; i <= a.length; i++) {
    System.out.println(a[i]);
}

Question: Explain which indexes the loop visits and why

Student's answer: i goes from 0 to a.length. Using <= or < makes no difference here, because both go through the whole array, so it visits each element once. Settings: width 3, depth 3, prune llm, backend claude-cli, model claude-opus-5-5

loop_control, misconceptions: 11 edges offered

Edges offered: | edge | |---| | err:loop_control->WrongIterationCount | wrong rule: Updates the loop counter so that the loop runs the wrong number of times. | right rule: The init, test and update together decide the number of passes; trace them to check the count. | | mis:loop_control->DoubleLoopIndexCount | wrong rule: for (double x = 0.0; x <= 1.0; x += 0.1) runs exactly 11 times. | right rule: Using a double as a for-loop index is legal but bad practice: the number of iterations depends on an equality test between double values, which may not give the result you expect. | | mis:loop_control->ForLoopPartSkipped | wrong rule: A pass of a loop may leave out one of its parts (the condition test, the body, the update, or the initialization). | right rule: Each pass of a for loop runs test, then body, then update, every time; the initialization runs once, at the start. | | mis:loop_control->ForUpdateBeforeBody | wrong rule: The update part of a for header (e.g. i = i - 4) runs before the body on each pass, so the first pass already sees the updated value. | right rule: The update runs after the body, before the next condition test; the first pass uses the initial value. | | mis:loop_control->IdiomOverridesCode | wrong rule: An array loop processes the whole array from index 0 to length-1 and increments its index at the end of the body, whatever the code says. | right rule: The loop visits exactly the indices that its initialisation, guard and update produce, in the order in which its statements are written. | | mis:loop_control->InfiniteLoopUnnoticed | wrong rule: A while loop always stops on its own, even if nothing in its body can make the condition false. | right rule: A while loop stops only when its condition is false at a check, so if no pass changes the variables in the condition, it never stops. | | mis:loop_control->LoopHeaderIsEquations | wrong rule: The initialization, condition and update of a for header are equations that all hold at the same time. | right rule: The three header parts are statements run at different moments: init once, then condition test, body, update, repeated. | | mis:loop_control->LoopStepAlwaysOne | wrong rule: A loop variable always goes up or down by 1, whatever the update says (so i = i - 4 is read as i--). | right rule: The loop variable changes exactly as the update expression says (i += 2, i = i - 4, i *= 2, ...). | | mis:loop_control->LoopUpdateChangesDirection | wrong rule: The update of the loop variable can change from pass to pass (e.g. switch direction) although the code is the same. | right rule: The update expression is the same on every pass; the loop variable changes by the rule written in the update. | | mis:loop_control->OffByOneBound | wrong rule: i < n and i <= n mean the same, so the loop runs until i equals n and the last pass can use a[n]. | right rule: for (i = 0; i < n; i++) runs n times with i going up to n - 1; with <= it runs n + 1 times and reaches i = n. | | mis:loop_control->PreIncrementBeforeLoop | wrong rule: With ++i in the update of for (int i = s; i < n; ++i), i is increased before the body runs, so the first pass uses s + 1. | right rule: The update runs after each pass of the body, so with either ++i or i++ the first pass uses i = s. |

(here mixing in: "++i in the for-update runs before the body each pass") | | lvl:loop_control@L1#0 | level L1 way names_the_element: Loop control is the init / continuation condition / increment scheme on an index variable that decides how many passes a loop makes and with which values. | | lvl:loop_control@L1#1 | level L1 way states_the_rule: Initialize an index variable, test a loop-continuation condition on it before each pass, and increment it as the last action of each pass; for (; ; ) packages the three. Choosing the loop: for when the passes are counted by an index, while when the loop runs until a condition changes, do-while when the body must run at least once; any one can be rewritten as another, so choose the clearest. | | lvl:loop_control@L2#0 | level L2 way line_by_line_trace: init (once) -> test -> body -> update -> test -> body -> update ... -> test false -> exit. | | lvl:loop_control@L2#1 | level L2 way output_prediction: The number of passes and the values seen follow from the three parts: for (int i = 0; once the condition is false the code after the loop runs once. | | mis:for_loop->ForInitRepeats | wrong rule: The initialization of a for loop runs again after a pass of the body. | right rule: The initialization runs exactly once, before the first condition test. | | mis:for_loop->ForIsConditional | wrong rule: The body of a for statement executes at most once. | right rule: The body of a for statement runs once for every pass on which the condition is true, which can be many times. | | mis:for_loop->ForLoopPartSkipped | wrong rule: A pass of a loop may leave out one of its parts (the condition test, the body, the update, or the initialization). | right rule: Each pass of a for loop runs test, then body, then update, every time; the initialization runs once, at the start. | | mis:for_loop->ForUpdateBeforeBody | wrong rule: The update part of a for header (e.g. i = i - 4) runs before the body on each pass, so the first pass already sees the updated value. | right rule: The update runs after the body, before the next condition test; the first pass uses the initial value. | | mis:for_loop->ForWhileNotInterchangeable | wrong rule: Some loops can only be written with for, others only with while. | right rule: Any for loop can be rewritten as a while loop and vice versa; for just packages init, test and update. | | mis:for_loop->IdiomOverridesCode | wrong rule: An array loop processes the whole array from index 0 to length-1 and increments its index at the end of the body, whatever the code says. | right rule: The loop visits exactly the indices that its initialisation, guard and update produce, in the order in which its statements are written. | | mis:for_loop->LoopCountIsStatementCount | wrong rule: The repeat count of a counted loop says how many of the body statements are executed. | right rule: The repeat count is how many times the whole body runs;
